messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: autoplot
parts:
At Hadley's suggestion, I wanted to bring a proposal discussion to the
wider ggplot community.

autoplot is the current distillation of some ideas that have been kicked
around in other forums. The idea is to create a framework for the
specification of complete plots of specific data structures using the
ggplot framework.

ggplot provides a framework for creating plots based on starting with
data, mapping data to aesthetics, scaling the data and aesthetics, and
providing a theming system for controlling plot appearance. At the same
time, many packages which create specific data structures, typically S3
or S4 objects, provide plot methods to graphically display them based,
typically, on base graphics. These default plots implement appropriate
conventions for the type of data plotted. A layer that is missing is the
ability to create a standard plot using ggplot so that it can be further
adjusted by setting scales, themes, etc. autoplot aims to fill this niche.

Most (though not all) of the current best understanding of how this
might work is contained in a page on the ggplot2 wiki
(https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/autoplot) and in a pull request
(https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/229) The pull request
references a "autoplot" branch of my fork of ggplot2 on github
(https://github.com/BrianDiggs/ggplot2/tree/autoplot) which I can accept
pull request on.

I invite everyone to look at the wiki page and respond with thoughts,
ideas, or examples where they have tried something like this and what
was learned from the attempt.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

[Bringing in ongoing discussion into this thread on the mailing list]

On 9/6/2011 4:53 AM, Ari Friedman wrote:
> Sorry for starting a discussion and then being MIA for so long. I
> looked for the continuation of this discussion in the mailing list
> but didn't see it so if someone could point me to the appropriate
> location that would be helpful.

That's because I just got around to creating it.

> If you have multiple data.frames could you put them into a list and
> then give them a class? So that the appropriate way to call it would
> be autoplot(my.new.classed.object).... It seems to me that most
> cases where you have multiple datasets that get combined in a
> particular way, it likely logically belongs in a class anyhow, even
> if it's a one-off class, since the data has a particular structure to
> it.

Well, if we want to continue the idiom of using fortify to convert some
data structure into a data.frame that is usable by ggplot, then a list
wouldn't work. Hadley's idea of a primary data.frame with secondary
data.frames as attributes is the one I like most so far.

> At the moment autoplot is spectacularly generic. That's probably a
> good thing. Perhaps the wiki could have an autoplot page under
> "Enhancing ggplot2" that would give guidelines for creating autoplot
> methods. One such guideline might be to first create a fortify
> method when possible, then to have autoplot call fortify. If fortify
> is not a good fit (no model, for instance), then I'd guess the
> simpler the better.

That's why I created the wiki page
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/autoplot. Unfortunately, it
shows up in the list of pages as "Summary" (since that was my original
first heading).

> Not sure what to do about passing arguments to different layers. I
> defer to the experts.

I think if there are a few different specific options for how the plot
could be rendered, they might make reasonable options to autoplot. But
not specific layer things; the idea is that you are dealing at a more
abstract level, which can then be modified at a lower level later.

> The return value is I think easier, since qplot does something
> similar. Just return all the ggplot2 objects. Since autoplot() when
> called from the command line should be print()'d automatically, it
> then will both produce the user-desired behavior (one-command
> plotting) and return a reasonable object which can then be layered on
> top of.

Agreed that the return type should be a ggplot2 object.

> Here's a quick example of one simple use case: replacing the pretty
> awful default plot of the microbenchmark package.
>
> library(taRifx)
> library(plyr)
> library(microbenchmark)
> library(ggplot2)
>
> dd<- data.frame(b = factor(c("Hi", "Med", "Hi", "Low"),
> levels = c("Low", "Med", "Hi"), ordered = TRUE),
> x = c("A", "D", "A", "C"), y = c(8, 3, 9, 9),
> z = c(1, 1, 1, 2))
> m<- microbenchmark(
> arrange(dd,desc(z),b),
> sort(dd, f= ~-z+b ),
> dd[with(dd, order(-z, b)), ] ,
> dd[order(-dd$z, dd$b),],
> times=100
> )
>
> #' Prettier plot of microbenchmark output using ggplot2's autoplot()
> #' @param x the microbenchmark object
> #' @param upper is a function to return the upper end of the range of
data drawn (by default it's the 75th percentile)
> #' @param lower is a function to return the lower end of the range of
data drawn (by default it's the 25th percentile)
> #' @param y_min is the lower bound of the plot range
> #' @param y_max is the upper bound of the plot range
> #' @return ggplot2 object
> #' @seealso \code{\link{autoplot}}
> #' @author Ari B. Friedman
\email{abfriedman@@gmail.com<http://gmail.com>}
> autoplot.microbenchmark<- function(x, upper = function(x)
quantile(x,prob=c(.75)), lower = function(x) quantile(x,prob=c(.25)),
y_min=0, y_max=max(by(x$time,x$expr,upper))*1.05, ...) {
> p<- ggplot(x,aes(x=expr,y=time)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c( y_min
, y_max ))
> p<- p + stat_summary( fun.y=median,fun.ymin = lower, fun.ymax =
upper, aes(fill=expr) )
> p
> }
>
> # Compare and contrast
> autoplot(m)
> plot(m)

Well, that is a bit unfair comparison because the plot method falls
through to plot.default; there is a boxplot.microbenchmark function
which is a better comparison (log scale by default, labeled axes).

microbenchmark is an easy example because the returned type already
inherits from data.frame:

> str(m)
Classes ï¿½microbenchmarkï¿½ and 'data.frame': 300 obs. of 2 variables:
$ expr: Factor w/ 3 levels "arrange(dd, desc(z), b)",..: 3 1 3 1 2 1 2
2 3 1 ...
$ time: num 464005 349715 290517 325762 293596 ...

(I used your example, but dropped on of the tests).

Here is how I would write autoplot.microbenchmarks (no documentation yet):

autoplot.microbenchmark <- function(x, ...) {
ggplot(x, aes(x=expr, y=time)) +
geom_boxplot() +
scale_x_discrete("Expression") +
scale_y_continuous("log(time) [ns]") +
coord_trans(y="log")
}


> Best wishes,
> Ari (gsk3)
